t: A Little-Known Trait Every Teacher Needs
q: Most teachers would benefit by cutting the amount of talking they do by one-third. Because talking too much causes students to tune you out.
By taking your time, by waiting, pausing, and moving more deliberately, your senses are better able to tune into the tone and temperature of your classroom.
It isn’t just important during periods of independent work. It’s important to have an observational mindset all the time .
When you’re stressed out, anxious, or worried, your breathing shallows. Your vision narrows. Your senses constrict.
Teachers who rush around, talk a lot, have narrow vision, and breathe in short, shallow breaths appear as if they don’t have their wits about them.
For many teachers, improving this one area is the missing ingredient. It’s the reason why they’ve felt as if nothing they do works as promised.

t: How To Handle Students Who Don’t Do Any Work
q: You see, by spending extra time with reluctant students, by coddling, appeasing, and buying into any of an unlimited number of justifications for their inaction, you create even more resistance.

Meanwhile, these same students who are assumed to be too attentive-averse or ill-equipped to succeed rush home at the end of another wasted day and play the same video game for three hours without a break.
You must be able to draw them in, absorb them in the moment, and maintain their state of flow— where time slows, mind-energy focuses, and concerns and worries of the past and future fade away.
Forcing their hand is the change-agent they desperately need to upend their downward trajectory.

Instead of rushing over with a huge smile and telling the student how wonderful they are because they completed a few sentences—which very effectively lowers the bar of expectation—point out their good work.
In the meantime, they’re a living and breathing reminder for you to be better.
x: Argues that coddling, bribing, and constant one-on-one help for reluctant workers enables their inaction and undermines their long-term motivation.

t: Do Routines Need To Be Done Perfectly?
q: In whatever way you teach and model how you expect your students to perform a given routine, then that’s how it should be done. In other words, it needs to be perfect under the parameters you’ve set.
Here at SCM, we believe that as long as there is no disruption to learning, you should allow for a level of freedom in your routines.
Therefore, if you want your students to be able to talk politely while entering your classroom, then you should allow it. A perfect routine isn’t one that matches the precision of a marching band.
The key to turning the vision of what you want your routines to look like into reality is in the teaching.
Then you redo the routine. You reteach it in even greater detail. You eliminate every last excuse and misunderstanding.
For elementary teachers this means extensive detailed modeling and practice in order to prove your students know for certain what a perfect routine for your classroom looks like.
x: Elementary teachers need extensive modeling and practice; middle and high school teachers rely more on clear verbal instruction as students age.
Responding to a common reader question, Linsin explains whether classroom routines need to be performed perfectly.
A 'perfect' routine is defined as one performed exactly as taught, not one that matches rigid, drill-instructor-style precision.
Routines are framed as central to reducing misbehavior, saving time, and freeing teachers to observe and supervise.
When a routine breaks down, the correct response is to reteach it in greater detail, not to lower expectations.

q: First, he sought to simplify. He aimed to reduce the complexity, as Stephen Ambrose writes in Supreme Commander, “into its essentials, extract a principal point, and then make that point his guiding star for all decisions.

But second (and more importantly for our purposes today), Eisenhower got all by himself and wrote about the situation until he had boiled it down to a single, guiding rule. “We must go unless there is a real and very serious deterioration in the weather,” he decided.

It’s this activity set — withdrawing to solitude, writing for clarity, and arriving at a rule through which to govern behavior when once again we return to the pressure of work — that I write to impress upon us today. This is the work that we need to become better at this coming school year, perhaps more than any other.

To live a life without rules creates only the illusion of freedom. Were I to allow myself to write only when I felt the pull, or work at any hour for the sake of my students, then I am certain I would be a less free man today than I am, not a freer one.
So it’s not just popular to disdain inflexible rules imposed from without — it’s dogma, enshrined in the very rubrics of our guild.
The evaluation rubric can’t be the final authority for the professional teacher; instead, one must follow a guiding rule derived from the hulk of one’s ever-growing professional expertise.

For you and me, I think that guiding rule is something like, “We must promote the long-term flourishing of young people by means of helping them master as much as possible this year, albeit none of this at the expense of our souls.

t: What To Say To A Needy, Dependent Student
q: Just be sure you keep some physical distance between you and them. Do not lean down, kneel next to them, or show any sympathy.
1. “You don’t need me.” 2. “You can do this.” 3. “I believe in you.
At first, yes. There is a chance they won’t get much done. But this is okay. It’s even good, because it’s really them.
Being forced, essentially, to either sit and do nothing or succeed, which you’ve prepared them for, is a powerful motivator to pursue the latter.
It cranks their intrinsic motivational engine on for the first time, turning their world upside down.

t: The Power of the Humdrum: Why Your First Day of School Isn’t Going to Make or Break Your School Year ke-or-break-your-school-year/
q: Great teachers did more than obsess on the efficiency of their classroom — their questions were artful; their assignments, demanding — but there was a clear tendency among positive outliers to see the power of the humdrum, the everyday.

I don’t remember a thing about Dr. Wong’s presentation. This was no fault of his, of course; I was just too scared to listen, so full were my head and heart with the ringing truism that the first day of school sets the course for all the 179 or so that follow it.

Thirteen years later, I can tell you that while of course first days and last days are special, they’re not omnipotent — not even close. What’s far more critical is the way in which you’ll use all the minutes allotted to you this year.

What matters, in other words, is what we make of the “humdrum,” of the everyday, those little minutes at the start and end and middle of our lessons. Those are 99% of the field in which we’ll sow (or not) the seeds of academic mastery.
The power of living well and teaching well is only accessible now. The well-being of the Stuart family isn’t found in which home we live in — it’s found in today’s humdrum moments.
But when the little quibbling creature comes crawling on your shoulder, do swat it away with the truth that the power isn’t in the first day or the last — it’s in all the minutes in between.
x: Quoting Practice Perfect on positive outliers who saw the power of the everyday, he says the humdrum minutes at the start, middle and end of lessons are 99 percent of the field where academic mastery is sown.
The piece advises preparing for the first day but swatting away the anxious urge to treat it as decisive, and it ends with a brief nod to a classroom management course.
The belief that day one makes or breaks the year is challenged by the point that first and last days are special but not omnipotent.
Most of the opportunity for academic mastery lies in the routine minutes of every lesson, a view supported by Practice Perfect's study of outlier teachers.
He illustrates the point with a personal story about feeling hurried to buy a home, concluding that the real well-being of his family lives in today's ordinary moments rather than in one big outcome.
Stuart's counsel is to prepare well for day one, then bring yourself back, day by day, to the power of the minutes available now.

t: “Stand and Practice? What Kind of PD is That?”
q: But Chris had an interesting bent toward leading professional development. Instead of just telling us about the intervention and giving us bits of time periodically in which to discuss it, he actually had us doing on odd thing.

Listening partner, your job will be to make 1-2 notes for feedback after the speaking partner is through with the simulation. After three minutes, we’ll sound a chime, and it’ll be time to switch roles.
Professional development as practice. That’s what Chris was doing. And amazingly, it was a semi-novel idea to me.

Sometimes we get stuck thinking of teaching as just an intellectual effort, but it’s hugely physical, too,” Lynsay explained. “So, if our goal is to get better at delivering clear instructions, say, or correcting misbehavior with emotional constancy, then these are things we’ve got to stand up and do, repeatedly, before we’re with students.

We realized that our workshop participants, on returning to their classrooms, were trying to do the equivalent of walking onto center court at Wimbledon and learning a new style of backhand in the midst of a match,” the authors write. “We realized… that we would have to approach teaching like tennis” (7).

For leaders, it seems to me that we must find opportunities to incorporate on-your-feet practice into our professional development sessions — just as Dr. Hulleman did at the workshop I attended. And for teachers, the next time you read something in a book or a blog post that you’d like to try, don’t wait until game time — stand up and practice it right then and there.

t: Why You Need To Give Frequent Reminders The First Week Of School
q: In fact, they’re examples of what you should never do —first week of school or not—because they’re reminders given after misbehavior has already begun.
The reason is that post-misbehavior reminders replace true accountability. They’re given instead of enforcing a consequence.
This very effectively makes misbehavior a hard choice for students rather than an impulsive act.
When you give pre-misbehavior reminders, you remove the awkwardness of enforcing consequences.
Your trust in them and their abilities will grow, and you’ll gradually shift more and more responsibility over to them with less input from you.
Before I say ‘go,’ remember to line up quietly and keep your hands to yourself.
x: Pre-misbehavior reminders during the first week largely eliminate common misbehaviors by removing excuses and forgetfulness.
Distinguishes harmful post-misbehavior reminders (a veiled threat that replaces accountability) from beneficial pre-misbehavior reminders.
As students demonstrate mastery of routines over time, the frequency of reminders should taper off, gradually shifting more responsibility onto the class.
Removing students' ability to claim confusion makes enforcing consequences easier and more consistent.
